title: California AI Laws
subtitle: AB 2013, SB 942, AB 3030, and more
body_html:
On this page

  • The pain California AI laws are causing our readers
  • The California AI laws stack, in operating order
  • Why California AI laws matter to you
  • What the research says about California AI laws
  • How to get compliant with California AI Laws: a 5-step path
  • Frequently asked questions about California AI laws
  • Primary sources on California AI laws

The one-paragraph answer

California AI laws are the largest stack of AI-specific legislation in the United States. California has not passed a single comprehensive AI act. Instead, it has passed dozens of targeted laws covering training data disclosure (AB 2013), AI content labeling (SB 942, operative since August 2, 2026, requiring generative AI providers with over 1,000,000 monthly users to offer a free AI detection tool and disclose AI-generated content), healthcare AI (AB 3030), employment AI, AI in political advertising, and generative AI transparency. Any company touching California users needs to comply with the stack, not just one law.

The pain California AI laws are causing our readers

Executives ask for "the California AI law." There is no single law. There is a stack. Companies operating in California, or with California users, are dealing with a rolling series of new obligations covering different slices of AI activity. Each law has its own effective date, its own definitions, its own enforcement mechanism, and its own penalty structure. Keeping the map current is a full-time compliance job.

The pain is stacking obligations without a unifying framework. Unlike the Colorado AI Act, which covers all "high-risk" AI in one law, California prefers narrow, targeted laws. That gives clearer scope per law but creates coordination cost across laws. Missing one because you thought you were compliant with another is a common failure pattern.

The California AI laws stack, in operating order

AB 2013 (Generative AI Training Data Transparency)

Signed in 2024, effective January 1, 2026. Requires developers of generative AI systems used or made available in California to post on their websites documentation about training data: sources, size, description, whether personal information or copyrighted material is included, and modifications made. Applies to models released or substantially modified from January 1, 2022 onward. Enforced by the California Attorney General.

SB 942 (California AI Transparency Act)

Signed in 2024, effective January 1, 2026. Requires "covered providers" of generative AI systems to provide free AI detection tools, apply latent disclosures to AI-generated content, and offer manifest disclosures on request. A covered provider is one whose system has over one million monthly California users.

AB 3030 (Healthcare AI Disclosure)

Signed in 2024, effective January 1, 2025. Requires healthcare providers using generative AI to communicate with patients about clinical information to disclose that AI was used and provide clear instructions for reaching a human. This is arguably the first US state law regulating clinical AI communications.

SB 1001 (Bolstering Online Transparency Act, "Bot Disclosure")

Effective 2019, ongoing. Requires bots that attempt to influence commercial or political decisions to identify themselves as bots. Applies to chatbots, automated messaging, and AI-driven agents.

AB 2655 and AB 2839 (Political AI)

Regulate AI-generated political content and deepfakes in elections, though implementation has been affected by ongoing First Amendment litigation. Companies whose products are used in political advertising need to track the status.

The CPPA's ADMT regulations, the biggest one nobody lists

The California Privacy Protection Agency finalised regulations on automated decision-making technology under the CCPA/CPRA. They are distinct from every statute above, and they are the closest thing California has to a comprehensive AI decision law. Businesses using ADMT for a significant decision (employment, lending, housing, education, healthcare) owe consumers pre-use notice, a right to opt out, and a right to access meaningful information about the logic. Risk assessments are required for higher-risk processing. Obligations phase in from 2027, with the first risk-assessment attestations due to the Agency thereafter.

If your California AI compliance plan covers AB 2013 and SB 942 but not the ADMT regulations, it is missing the piece that most closely resembles the Colorado regime that was repealed. California kept, through its privacy agency, roughly what Colorado gave up.

Employment AI laws

California civil rights agencies have issued regulations under existing state anti-discrimination law that apply to AI in employment decisions. The California Civil Rights Council's automated-decision-systems regulations effectively add impact assessment and bias testing obligations to any employer using AI in hiring, promotion, or termination decisions in California.

Why California AI laws matter to you

California has 39 million residents, the world's fifth-largest economy, and a plaintiffs' bar highly active in consumer protection and privacy litigation. Any AI system used by California residents is potentially in scope. Enforcement risk is real (the California Attorney General, the California Civil Rights Department, and city attorneys all have enforcement authority). Private right of action exists for several laws in the stack.

California AI laws also shape national practice by market force. When a large software company complies with California's stack for California users, it usually applies the compliance uniformly across all users because segregating by state is impractical. This means California AI laws effectively set the national floor for many AI transparency obligations.

What the research says about California AI laws

The academic literature on California AI laws is ahead of most corporate practice, and it is unusually blunt. Two findings are worth putting in front of any executive who thinks this is a compliance formality.

“concerns about their impact on individual and societal wellbeing, particularly due to the lack of transparency and accountability”

Cheong, Frontiers in Human Dynamics (2024)

That is the gap between having AI and governing it. The second finding is the one that tends to change the room.

“all those who are involved in the research, development and maintenance of AI systems have social and ethical responsibilities”

Camilleri, Expert Systems (2023)

Neither of these is a fringe position. Both come from peer-reviewed work, and both describe the condition most organisations are actually in when the question about California AI laws arrives from the board, the buyer, or the regulator.

How to get compliant with California AI Laws: a 5-step path

This is the sequence that works, and it is not the sequence most organisations choose. They start with the framework and work backwards toward reality. Start with reality.

  1. Inventory the AI in scope. List every AI system that could fall under California AI laws. Record what it does, what decision it influences, what data it touches, and who owns it. You cannot govern AI you cannot name, and almost every organisation we assess is running more AI than its leadership believes.
  2. Determine whether you are actually in scope. Work out precisely which of your AI systems and activities California AI laws reaches, and write the determination down with its reasoning. Do this in writing. A documented scope determination, right or wrong, is defensible. An undocumented assumption is not.
  3. Assign one accountable owner. Name a person, not a committee, with the authority to stop a deployment. Governance without someone who can say no is documentation, not control.
  4. Build the evidence file. Assemble the documentation California AI laws expects: the scope, the risk assessment, the controls, the testing evidence, and the incident record. Assemble it before anyone asks. Reconstructing it under a regulator's deadline costs several times more and looks exactly like what it is.
  5. Set a review cadence and hold it. Re-run the assessment on a schedule and after any material change to the model, the data, or the use case. Alignment decays. A control tested once is a snapshot, not a control.

Done in this order, California AI laws becomes tractable. Done out of order, it becomes a document nobody uses and a control nobody exercises.

Frequently asked questions about California AI laws

Do we need to comply if we are not based in California?

Yes, if California residents use your AI systems. Extraterritorial reach is the norm, not the exception.

Which of the California AI laws is the most urgent?

For generative AI providers, AB 2013 and SB 942 both take effect January 1, 2026, so both need attention now. For healthcare organizations, AB 3030 is already in effect (January 2025). For employers, the California Civil Rights Council regulations are in effect now.

How do California AI laws interact with CCPA/CPRA?

CCPA/CPRA covers personal data. California AI laws cover AI decision-making and transparency. Many systems trigger both. Integrated compliance is required.

Where do California AI laws fit in SRJ's work?

The AI Business Enablement Audit™ includes a California-specific compliance overlay. Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library™ maps operating artifacts to individual California statutes in Appendix L.

Primary sources on California AI laws

The authoritative texts and agency pages behind this summary. We keep this page current, but where a compliance decision turns on exact wording, read the source. Anything concerning California AI laws that carries legal consequence should be confirmed against the enrolled text or the issuing body, not against a secondary summary, including this one.

  • California Legislative Information

Enacted AI laws in California

20 laws this site judged relevant to AI, newest first, each read from its enrolled text.

  • SB503: Health care services: artificial intelligence. passed 2026-09-30

    Requires developers and deployers of clinical decision support systems, which are artificial intelligence systems that aid clinical decisionmaking related to timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment, to identify systems with known or reasonably foreseeable risk of biased impacts, requires developers to mitigate those risks and provide documentation to deployers, and requires deployers to monitor and mitigate those risks.

  • SB1159: Artificial intelligence: transparency and governance. passed 2026-09-30

    This law clarifies that under specified California transparency and governance laws, terms such as person, interested person, participant, and member of the public do not include artificial intelligence systems, autonomous agents, or robots. It prohibits a person from knowingly using artificial intelligence to falsely represent that a natural person engaged with a governmental agency. It also authorizes governmental agencies to use disclosure verification tools to detect artificial intelligence.

  • SB1000: California AI Transparency Act. passed 2026-09-30

    This bill amends the California AI Transparency Act to remove the user threshold from the definition of covered provider, replace the AI detection tool with a disclosure verification tool, remove the requirement to offer a manifest disclosure option, and require latent disclosures to state whether the GenAI system created or altered the content. It delays application to GenAI systems designed primarily as assistive technology until January 1, 2029, prohibits false assistive technology claims with a separate civil penalty, and takes effect immediately as an urgency statute.

  • AB1979: Health care services: artificial intelligence. passed 2026-09-30

    This act adds Chapter 25.5 to the Business and Professions Code requiring health facilities, clinics, physician offices, and group practice offices to preserve licensed health care providers' independent professional judgment when using clinical decision support systems and prohibits using artificial intelligence to independently perform licensed clinical functions or direct unlicensed personnel. It also amends the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act to treat businesses offering health care chatbots as providers of health care subject to that act's confidentiality requirements and penalties.

  • AB2392: Public postsecondary education: generative artificial intelligence systems: procurement standards: training. passed 2026-09-30

    This law requires the California Community Colleges and the California State University, and requests the University of California, to jointly convene an intersegmental working group to develop procurement standards and training for generative artificial intelligence systems. The working group must develop minimum protections for procured systems and training content, and present recommendations by January 1, 2028. The segments must provide the training, review and update it annually, maintain training records, and report on systemwide GenAI contracts until procurement standards are adopted.

  • AB2713: California AI Transparency Act: system provenance data. passed 2026-09-30

    Amends the California AI Transparency Act to require large online platforms to detect provenance data on distributed content, provide a user interface indicating whether content was generated or substantially altered by a GenAI system or captured by a capture device, allow users to inspect system provenance data, and prohibit knowingly stripping system provenance data or digital signatures. It also clarifies that obligations apply only to data compliant or interoperable with widely adopted specifications from an established standards-setting body and does not require handling personal information.

  • SB947: Employment: automated decision systems. passed 2026-09-30

    This part regulates employer use of automated decision systems in employment. It prohibits certain uses of ADS, requires human corroboration for disciplinary or termination decisions primarily based on ADS output, and mandates employee data access and postuse notice. It provides enforcement by the Labor Commissioner and public prosecutors, with civil penalties and remedies.

  • AB1609: Customer service chatbots. passed 2026-09-28

    This chapter prohibits large private businesses from representing that a customer service chatbot is a human and requires a clear disclosure when a reasonable person would likely be misled. It requires large private businesses to provide a customer service feature to request a human agent during regular business hours and to make good faith efforts to connect within 15 minutes or schedule an appointment, with limits on hold times. It authorizes public prosecutors to enforce and imposes civil penalties, with no private right of action.

  • AB2504: Community colleges: artificial intelligence: pilot program. passed 2026-09-18

    This law establishes the Future of Creative Industries Pilot Program within the California Community Colleges. The program supports workers in creative and entertainment industries who have been or are at risk of being displaced by generative artificial intelligence through reskilling and upskilling opportunities. It requires a report to the Legislature by January 1, 2032, and repeals the program on January 1, 2033.

  • SB1119: Companion chatbots: children’s safety. passed 2026-09-10

    This law, known as Adam's Law, requires operators of companion chatbots to assess and mitigate child safety risks before making new or substantially modified chatbots available in California. It imposes age determination, child safety policies, default settings, parental controls, crisis protocols, data and advertising restrictions, and independent child safety audits. It authorizes enforcement by public prosecutors and private civil actions for actual harm to children.

  • SB867: Toys: companion chatbots. passed 2026-09-10

    This law amends Section 22601 of the Business and Professions Code to define terms and adds Section 22604.5. It prohibits any person from manufacturing, selling, exchanging, possessing with intent to sell or exchange, or exposing or offering for sale or exchange to a retailer any toy that includes a companion chatbot. The prohibition is temporary and is repealed on January 1, 2031.

  • SB813: Independent verification organizations. passed 2026-09-09

    This chapter requires the Government Operations Agency, on or before January 1, 2028, to develop application requirements, suspension and termination procedures, and qualification criteria for independent verification organizations, or IVOs, which are AI auditors designated by the agency as having demonstrated expertise in assessing AI risks. It requires the agency to consult stakeholders, convene working groups, and report to the Legislature, and requires designated IVOs to submit annual reports. It also states that the chapter does not require AI developers, deployers, or operators to engage an IVO or undergo a covered AI audit, and that audit evidence is relevant but not conclusive in harm actions.

  • AB1405: Artificial intelligence: auditors: registration. passed 2026-09-09

    This chapter requires the Government Operations Agency to establish an AI Auditor Registry by January 1, 2029, set annual registration fees, and create a mechanism for reporting misconduct by registered AI auditors. Beginning January 1, 2029, it prohibits offering, selling, or conducting a covered AI audit unless registered with the agency. It imposes registration, reporting, independence, retention, and whistleblower protection requirements on registered AI auditors and authorizes removal from the registry and referral to enforcement authorities for violations.

  • AB1651: State Bar of California: artificial intelligence. passed 2026-08-22

    This law requires the State Bar of California to disclose when it uses artificial intelligence generated content in developing or administering the State Bar examinations and in study materials it prepares, publishes, endorses, or distributes. The disclosure requirement applies only to content developed by or at the explicit direction of the State Bar and applies even if a natural person revises or reviews the content. The law becomes operative on January 1, 2028.

  • AB621: Deepfake pornography. passed 2025-10-13

    This law gives a depicted individual a private right of action against anyone who creates and intentionally discloses, or intentionally discloses, digitized sexually explicit material without consent or involving a minor, and against anyone who knowingly facilitates or recklessly aids or abets that conduct. It defines deepfake pornography services, creates presumptions of liability for service owners and enablers, increases statutory damages, and allows public prosecutors to bring civil enforcement actions.

  • SB243: Companion chatbots. passed 2025-10-13

    This law regulates companion chatbot platforms in California. It requires operators to notify users when a companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human if a reasonable person would be misled, to maintain and publish protocols to prevent suicidal ideation, suicide, or self harm content, and to provide special protections for known minor users. It also requires annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention beginning July 1, 2027, and creates a private right of action for injury in fact.

  • AB853: California AI Transparency Act. passed 2025-10-13

    This act delays the operative date of the California AI Transparency Act to August 2, 2026. Beginning January 1, 2027, it requires large online platforms to detect and disclose provenance data for distributed content and prohibits them from stripping that data, and it prohibits GenAI hosting platforms from knowingly making available GenAI systems that do not place disclosures. Beginning January 1, 2028, it requires capture device manufacturers to provide a user option for latent disclosures and to embed latent disclosures by default in certain capture devices.

  • AB489: Health care professions: deceptive terms or letters: artificial intelligence. passed 2025-10-11

    This chapter makes existing prohibitions on using specified health care professional titles, letters, or phrases enforceable against developers and deployers of artificial intelligence or generative artificial intelligence systems that use those terms in advertising or functionality. It also prohibits AI or GenAI technology from indicating or implying that care, advice, reports, or assessments are provided by a natural person with the appropriate health care license or certificate. Each prohibited use is a separate violation subject to the appropriate health care professional licensing board.

  • AB979: California Cybersecurity Integration Center: artificial intelligence. passed 2025-10-03

    The law requires the California Cybersecurity Integration Center to develop, by January 1, 2027, a California AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook in consultation with the Office of Information Security and the Government Operations Agency. The playbook must include mandatory information sharing mechanisms for state contractors and vendors providing AI services about threats and vulnerabilities in those services, and may include voluntary mechanisms for other entities. Information shared under the playbook related to cyber threat indicators or defensive measures is confidential and may only be shared with approved state employees and contractors.

  • SB53: Artificial intelligence models: large developers. passed 2025-09-29

    The Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act requires large frontier developers to publish and follow a frontier AI framework, publish transparency reports before deploying frontier models, and report critical safety incidents and internal use catastrophic risk assessments to the Office of Emergency Services. It also creates whistleblower protections for covered employees of frontier developers and establishes a consortium to develop a framework for a public cloud computing cluster called CalCompute. Civil penalties of up to one million dollars per violation are enforceable only by the Attorney General.
